points.en: The counselor should spend about two-thirds of the session listening and only about one-third speaking.
It matters because it suppresses the pastor's urge to teach and fix, letting the real story, buried under shame, emerge rather than the first surface story.
Undivided attention is the first restoration for an isolated, troubled person.
It is open-ended: it cannot be answered yes or no and lets the counselee begin where, how fast and in how much detail he chooses.
Closed questions narrow the conversation too soon and make the counselee confirm or deny a frame the counselor supplied.
The five attitudes are evaluative (judging), interpretive (imposing meaning), supportive (soothing), probing (seeking information) and understanding (checking one has heard correctly).
The understanding response is the gold standard of Step Two.
Each other attitude has a hazard if overused: evaluating stops honesty, interpreting short-circuits discovery, reassuring or probing too much overwhelms or interrogates.
James 1:19 sets the order swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath, and hearing must precede speaking.
Step Two's listening discipline puts this into practice: the counselor holds back speech and judgment so that he responds to what he has actually heard.
Gives three responses that reflect or paraphrase her own words and feelings about the mother-in-law, checking understanding.
None tells her what she really means (interpretive), pushes the marriage topic, judges, reassures or asks a probing question.
Speaking half the time breaks the two-thirds rule: the counselor is managing the talk rather than listening, perhaps evaluating, interpreting or probing too much.
He adjusts deliberately: talks less, uses short cues and understanding reflections, lets silence stand, and hands the floor back.
He asks why he was talking so much, e.g. his own discomfort or enjoying being needed.
The reply is evaluative: after a thin acknowledgement it moves to a judgment, using what wives should do, and also uses Scripture too early.
Harm: evaluation before she is heard makes her stop telling the truth and withdraw, and Scripture used to close her down erodes trust.
A better response reflects her feeling of being unimportant to her overworked husband and delays teaching until she is fully heard.
Proverbs 18:13 calls answering before hearing folly and shame; the two-thirds rule applies this by making the counselor hear before he speaks.
Speaking first leads to answers aimed at the wrong problem and leaves the counselee unheard, whereas listening first expresses humility and respect.
The temptation is to fill the silence with a question or comfort, because even 30 seconds feels long and uncomfortable to an inexperienced counselor.
The discipline is to wait attentively, since the counselee may be gathering courage for a breakthrough and filling the silence would lose it.
He recognizes the discomfort as his own, keeps his body present, and trusts the Spirit to work in the quiet.
Understanding responses could be misused as a technique, e.g. to disarm defenses, extract disclosures or steer the counselee toward the counselor's own conclusion.
The guard is the counselor's character: genuine love and integrity before God, remembering the conversation is not for him, and showing only honest responses.
